key: Come now, and let us reason together, Saith the LORD; Though your sins be as scarlet, They shall be as white as snow; Though they be red like crimson, They shall be as wool.
s: After the LORD refuses Judah’s offerings and bids it cease from evil and plead for the widow, an appeal follows; Rashi, on 1:18, reads it as God and Israel weighing together who wronged whom, hope of repentance still held out, and Ibn Ezra, on 1:18, as the prophet bidding Israel join him in accepting God’s rebuke.

evidence.words: לכו נא ונוכחה. יחד אני ואתם ונדע מי סרח על מי ואם אתם סרחתם עלי עודני נותן לכם תקוה לשוב … יש אומר כי ונוכחה דברי השם … והנכון בעיני שהוא דברי הנביא לישראל, כאומרו השם אמר לי שנקבל תוכחת
evidence.gloss: [Rashi, on 1:18, ‘Come now, and let us reason’:] Together, I and you, and we shall know who has offended against whom; and if you have offended against Me, I still give you hope to return … [Ibn Ezra, on 1:18, ‘let us reason’:] Some say that ‘let us reason’ is the words of God … and what is right in my eyes is that it is the prophet’s words to Israel, as though he said: God told me that we should accept rebuke.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Isaiah 1:18, at [334,18]); one unit, 34 words, no dash. Plain sense faithful to day.js: 1:11 to 1:15 refuse the sacrifices, new moons and prayers, 1:16 to 1:17 bid them cease to do evil and plead for the widow, and 1:18 follows as the appeal; no four-word repeat of the key. Rashi on 1:18 (lemma לכו נא ונוכחה) reads it as I and you together, to know who offended whom, with hope to return still given: the sentence carries it. Ibn Ezra on 1:18 reports that some take ונוכחה as God’s words and holds his own view that it is the prophet’s words to Israel, that we accept rebuke (Friedlander’s English: we, you Israel and I): the sentence carries it. The two genuinely differ on who speaks and the sentence names both without resolving. Radak and Metzudat David also read; Midrash empty. Entry passes entry-check; src names each edition.
